meta.title: Olavo de Carvalho — Cronologia
meta.subtitle: Chronology of Olavo de Carvalho (1947–2022): life and works
meta.description: An open, source-referenced chronology of Olavo de Carvalho — journalist, astrologer, self-taught philosopher, teacher of the Curso Online de Filosofia, and the central intellectual reference of the Brazilian New Right.
meta.dataQualityNote: Work-in-progress dataset compiled from public sources (see references). Contested claims — above all his influence on the Bolsonaro government, the cause of his death, and the episodes of his early trajectory — are attributed to their authors, never asserted in this site's voice. Dates not verified against a primary source are flagged. Corrections against primary sources are welcome.

threads.note: These lanes are an editorial reading of a contested life, not a neutral fact: the currents are the ones he himself named as his formation — in a 2012 lecture he called it his great sin to have spent 'thirty-some years absorbing all the influences' (per the community transcriptions) — plus the public roles the record documents. Lanes are containers for dated events, never a claim that the currents weigh the same. Left out as lanes, deliberately: family life (private; it appears only where already public), the transcription corpus's internal scholarship (its own project), and the Brazilian New Right ecosystem around him (a distinct, living-persons subject).

lanes.label: Illness & the body
lanes.basis: His own repeated origin story — sick from birth, seven years bedridden — which he himself tied to his drive to understand human situations (lectures of 2010-10-09 and after), through the 2018 surgery and the final year.

lanes.label: Journalism & the press
lanes.basis: His own periodization of his livelihood (working from 14, journalism at 17 for the five-hour day; lecture of 2010-11-13) and the press-career record (obituaries; the Comunique-se profile).

lanes.label: Communist youth
lanes.basis: His own bracketing (1964 not yet militant; 'twenty years cleaning it out') and the BBC Brasil interview profile's 1966–1968.

lanes.label: Astrology & the esoteric quest
lanes.basis: His own master list of the seeker years (lecture of 2012-09-08: psychoanalyses, New Age, Rosicrucians, astrology, 'macumbas', Islamic esoterism) and Calil's account of the Escola Júpiter period.

lanes.label: Traditionalism & the tariqa
lanes.basis: Mark Sedgwick's scholarship of the Maryamiyya episode and his own tellings (met Schuon 1986, muqaddam on arrival, about a year and a half).

lanes.label: Catholic return
lanes.basis: His own dated lecture statements (Padre Paulo Ricardo named his personal confessor, 2010-10-30; confession practice into 2020) and the deathbed-sacraments account.

lanes.label: Philosophy & teaching
lanes.basis: The works record (the 1994–96 books onward, the Seminário, the 585-lecture COF) and his self-periodization: teaching since 1989, first book at 48.

lanes.label: Politics & attributed influence
lanes.basis: Press and academic characterizations — always attributed, and rejected by him in his own dated words — plus his documented 2020–21 rift statements.

facts.label: Who
facts.value: Olavo Luiz Pimentel de Carvalho — journalist, professional astrologer in the 1980s, self-taught philosopher and polemicist; from 2009 teacher of the Curso Online de Filosofia (COF)

facts.label: Died
facts.value: Night of 24 January 2022, in a hospital in the Richmond, Virginia area (USA), aged 74; announced by the family in the early hours of 25 January. The cause was publicly disputed — see the chronology

facts.label: Residency
facts.value: Brazilian citizen; resident in the United States (Richmond, Virginia area) from 2005 until his death; buried at St. Joseph's Cemetery, Petersburg, Virginia

facts.label: Decorations
facts.value: Medalha do Pacificador (Brazilian Army, 1999); Medalha Mérito Santos Dumont (Brazilian Air Force, 2001); Grã-Cruz of the Ordem de Rio Branco (2019 — contested, see chronology)

facts.label: Family
facts.value: Married to Roxane Andrade de Souza; eight children and eighteen grandchildren at his death

events.title: Born in Campinas, São Paulo
events.text: Born Olavo Luiz Pimentel de Carvalho. Obituaries note he had little formal schooling and described himself as self-taught.

events.title: Childhood illness — his own account
events.text: His most repeated origin story in the course: sick from birth and bedridden through his first seven years with constant fever, then suddenly and inexplicably cured around age seven, going straight to school afterward (told, among other places, in the lectures of 9 October 2010 and 20 April 2013). In a lecture of 16 January 2010 he added that he was born with an undiagnosed tracheal tumor still with him in his sixties; in a lecture of c. 2020 he tied his late-diagnosed emphysema to a lung operation decades earlier. All of this is his own retrospective testimony via the community transcriptions, unverified against audio — recorded here as testimony, not as a medical record. A second line of his own testimony describes the condition itself, twice. On 10 August 2009 he said he had been born with a tracheal tumour and an infectious bronchitis that was near-fatal for seven years — though a fortnight later he said instead that nobody had known what he had, a wobble worth recording rather than smoothing. Again on his programme of 14 April 2010 — eight years before the surgery and twelve before his death — he said he had been born with a tracheal tumour, which he sized by comparison to an orange. In the same passage he said he had smoked since fifteen, three packs a day for over forty years. Both are his own statements in machine-transcribed broadcasts and neither is a medical record; the first is the earliest first-person account yet found of the congenital condition that the 2018 surgery would remove, and it long predates the disputes that followed his death.

events.title: Brief affiliation with the Brazilian Communist Party (PCB)
events.text: A BBC Brasil profile built on an in-person interview (Fellet, December 2016) states 'Entre 1966 e 1968, militou no Partido Comunista'; the historian Gilberto Calil records a brief PCB passage in the 1960s without exact dates. The dating rests on his own recollection as relayed by the interviewer, so the flag stays. In the course he bracketed the period himself: in 1964 he was a secondary student with vague leftist sympathy, not yet a militant, and he recalled joining the party 'to stir up trouble' and spending twenty years working the influence out of himself (lectures of 2009 and 2014, per the community transcriptions).

events.title: First contributions to Folha de S.Paulo
events.text: Both Wikipedias date his first Folha de S.Paulo piece (in the Folhetim section, on The Magic Flute) to February 1977. Other sources push his journalism back earlier — Gazeta do Povo says he started at 17 at Folha da Manhã; Calil says he began writing for major newspapers in 1967. The sources do not reconcile these, and they may describe different roles. His own telling in the course: working from age 14 to ease his mother's burden, and entering journalism at 17 expressly because the legal five-hour day left time to study (lecture of 13 November 2010, among others), with the professional registry later obtained by time of service.

events.title: Co-founds the Escola Júpiter de Astrologia
events.text: Worked professionally as an astrologer c. 1979–1982, co-founding the school and its Revista de Astrologia Júpiter and collaborating on a university-extension astrology course at PUC-SP; Calil (2021) reports the school had about 140 students by 1980. He later abandoned and disavowed astrology. His own telling in the course: professionally an astrologer for about two years, with some 5,000 charts interpreted — psychiatrists sent him patients' horoscopes — and the school closing around 1980; he quit after judging the techniques unserious.

events.title: First book: A Imagem do Homem na Astrologia
events.text: The 1980 date belongs to a 38-page booklet (Ed. Júpiter), grown out of the 1979 PUC-SP astrology course. Olavo's own CV opens its 'Livros publicados' list with three 1983 titles (Speculum) — which explains Agência Brasil's 'first book, 1983': the two dates describe different things (a course booklet vs. his first books proper). The 1980 edition is attested only by book-trade listings, so the flag stays.

events.title: Enters the Traditionalist / Perennialist milieu
events.text: Per Calil (2021), around 1982 he joined an esoteric 'Tradition' group. Sedgwick's peer-reviewed history of Brazilian Traditionalism (2021) documents the arc: an interest in Traditionalism from 1977, after he was given Jacob Needleman's anthology The Sword of Gnosis; Michel Veber's 1980 lecture on Guénon at the Escola Júpiter and a further series in 1981; his own translation of Guénon's La Métaphysique orientale (A Metafísica Oriental, Escola Júpiter, 1981); an article in the New Age magazine Planeta (no. 107, August 1981) calling Veber 'my professor' — in which he also wrote that Veber had studied under Guénon's personal guidance, which Sedgwick notes was impossible, Veber having been four years old when Guénon left France in 1930; the founding of an Instituto de Estudos Tradicionais; and the first Traditionalist article to appear in a major Brazilian newspaper, 'Moralidade sem Deus?' (Jornal da Tarde, 27 February 1982). He also led followers into A Tradição, the organization of Omar Ali Shah, and broke with it after concluding its leader was a 'con-man' (Sedgwick, quoting his term) — a public dispute that reached the police. Approximate dating for the group entry itself; all characterizations are these scholars'.

events.title: Involvement with Sufi Islam (the Maryamiyya of Frithjof Schuon)
events.text: Calil (2021) states he converted to Islam in 1984, took the name Sidi Mohammad Ibrahim, and set up a tariqa of his own that dissolved within months. Sedgwick (2021) documents the sequence from the Lings correspondence: after contacting Marco Pallis, Carvalho and some of his followers corresponded with Martin Lings, who explained that 'entering Islam' was the appropriate preparation for the Maryami tariqa — which they did. Lings's letters address him as 'Sidi Muhammad' from June 1985; they were deposited at the São Paulo state court in 1990 as evidence in a case brought by a former follower, which Carvalho won. Sedgwick places him at the 1985 Traditionalist conference in Lima where Lings was present, but marks that presence as deduced rather than documented; he records that in 1986 Carvalho led a group of Brazilians to Bloomington, Indiana, where Schuon appointed him muqaddam (Sufi representative) for Brazil. Carvalho himself later said he had 'entered' Islam rather than converted, in Guénon's sense. On the exit Sedgwick is only relative — 'within a few years' he became disenchanted, telling an interviewer he had discovered that Schuon backed a rival for the leadership of the Brazilian Maryamiyya and had endorsed rumours against him — which converges with his own telling in the course: met Schuon in 1986, made muqaddam on arrival, stayed about a year and a half, provoked his own expulsion, placing the exit around 1987–88 (per the community transcriptions). He later disavowed the period's books as reflecting 'more a duty of obedience' to Schuon than his own thought.

events.title: Publishes Fronteiras da Tradição, his first book beyond astrology
events.text: Lectures from his Traditionalist teaching period — several first given at the Editora Astrociência in Rio de Janeiro — are published as Fronteiras da Tradição (São Paulo: Nova Stella, 1986), per Sedgwick (2021) his first book on a topic other than astrology. Its references are 'almost without exception' the major Traditionalist authors; it urges an orthodox religion as the exoteric frame for esoteric practice and warns against pseudo-initiatic organizations, citing A Tradição as an example. The volume also reprints the 1982 Jornal da Tarde article.

events.title: Publishes A Nova Era e a Revolução Cultural
events.text: On Gramsci and Fritjof Capra (Instituto de Artes Liberais); obituaries treat it as the book that established him as a conservative polemicist.

events.title: Publishes O Jardim das Aflições
events.text: Subtitled 'de Epicuro à ressurreição de César' (Diadorim); later republished, and the source of the 2017 documentary's title.

events.title: Publishes O Imbecil Coletivo
events.text: His polemic against the Brazilian intelligentsia ('atualidades inculturais brasileiras'); Calil (2021) notes it achieved significant circulation and made him a public figure.

events.title: Publishes Aristóteles em Nova Perspectiva
events.text: His 'theory of the four discourses' reading of Aristotle (Topbooks); year and publisher rest on a single tertiary source.

events.title: Receives the Medalha do Pacificador (Brazilian Army)
events.text: Reported in Agência Brasil's obituary career summary.

events.title: Receives the Medalha Mérito Santos Dumont (Brazilian Air Force)
events.text: Reported in Agência Brasil's obituary career summary.

events.title: Founds the website Mídia Sem Máscara
events.text: A media-criticism site against what it described as leftist bias in the Brazilian press; Calil (2021) treats it as his main ideological platform from 2002 until it went offline around 2017.

events.title: Records the Curso História Essencial da Filosofia — already its fifth delivery
events.text: An eight-session history-of-philosophy course, videotaped by the publisher É Realizações, running from the pre-Socratics to the advent of Christianity. He dates it on the recordings themselves and says he has already taught it four times, the first in Rio in 1993 — so this is a fifth delivery of a course a decade old, not a new one. It is taught live and in person, in the same room as his separate Seminário de Filosofia, which he mentions meets the following day: the seminar therefore existed in Brazil three years before he emigrated. The recordings are the fullest systematic statement of his reading of the philosophers before the Curso Online de Filosofia begins in 2009, and the printed collection drawn from them runs to 2006.

events.title: Moves to the United States
events.text: Settled in the Richmond, Virginia area, where he lived until his death; the date is given consistently across obituaries and profiles.

events.title: Begins the online radio program True Outspeak
events.text: First episode aired 4 December 2006 — preserved with the show's own audio and a transcript ('estamos inaugurando o nosso programa') in an Internet Archive collection; Calil (2021) confirms the program. It ran on BlogTalkRadio until 2013 per English Wikipedia.

events.place: São Paulo, Brazil (taught from the United States)
events.title: Teaching Brazil by videoconference from the United States
events.text: His own telling on the True Outspeak broadcasts of April 2007: the Seminário de Filosofia he had been running in Brazil since at least 2002 was by then reaching São Paulo by videoconference from the United States, hosted at É Realizações, and he announced a session for the 18th of that month. In February 2007 he put the teaching in a longer line — courses 'for twenty years', which he said he was continuing by videoconference — and listeners wrote in as students. What changed after the 2005 emigration was therefore the delivery, not the teaching: the Curso Online de Filosofia of 2009 industrialized an operation that had already crossed the Atlantic. Recorded as self-testimony from machine-transcribed broadcasts, not as an institutional record.

events.title: First lecture of the Curso Online de Filosofia (COF)
events.text: The paid weekly online philosophy course he taught until his death — 585 lectures over thirteen years. A student index and English Wikipedia date the first class to 14 March 2009. The community transcription corpus of the course is public (see references); this project cites it by aula and date only. His own broadcasts bracket the launch closely: on 9 March 2009 he announced the first class for 'next Saturday, the 14th', and a week later reported that they had expected about a hundred people and more than four hundred arrived, collapsing the streaming provider and forcing the bandwidth to be widened. The start had slipped for five months — promised 'next month' in December 2008, then 'February, March at the latest' in January, then 'a week, ten days at most' in late February — and the delivered format was a members-only stream with an open Brazilian phone line rather than the Skype arrangement he had described in October 2008. It began fortnightly and was weekly by that August.

events.title: Founds the Inter-American Institute for Philosophy, Government, and Social Thought
events.text: Founded in late 2009 (its web domain was registered 10 December 2009 and it operated as a Virginia 501(c)(3), per IRS records); Olavo served as president. He announced its closure himself on 29 November 2018 ('Fechei o Interamerican...'), reported by the press days later.

events.title: Names Padre Paulo Ricardo as his personal confessor
events.text: In the lecture of 30 October 2010 he described Padre Paulo Ricardo de Azevedo as his personal confessor; a year earlier (28 November 2009) he had called him the only priest in Brazil he trusted, and in May 2010 he recounted the priest's recent visit to his Virginia home. Together with his stated practice of confession as late as 2020 and the sacraments received on his deathbed (reported by Silvio Grimaldo of Brasil Sem Medo), this documents in his own dated words his return to full Catholic practice during the US years. The origin of that return — accounts circulate of a c. 2006 visit — remains unverified and is told differently by sympathetic and hostile sources.

events.title: Written debate with Aleksandr Dugin begins
events.text: The Carvalho–Dugin debate on 'The USA and the New World Order' ran online from 4 March to 31 July 2011, when both published their conclusions; the host site was reportedly accessed by some 200,000 people from over thirty countries. Sedgwick (2021) reads it as a debate about global politics rather than doctrine: Dugin began it believing he was debating a fellow Brazilian Traditionalist and ended disappointed, while Carvalho showed no interest in common ground — 'the debate, then, was not really about Traditionalism at all'.

events.title: The Dugin debate is published as Os EUA e a Nova Ordem Mundial
events.text: Portuguese edition of the debate (VIDE Editorial, trans. Giuliano Moraes); still sold by the official Seminário de Filosofia bookstore.

events.title: Publishes O Mínimo que Você Precisa Saber para Não Ser um Idiota
events.text: 193 press articles from 1997–2013, organized by Felipe Moura Brasil (Record). A best-seller: English Wikipedia cites c. 320,000 copies; Poder360 reports 400,000 combined with O Imbecil Coletivo by 2019 — the figures differ.

events.title: His YouTube channel is created
events.text: The channel's own About page records 'Joined Jul 7, 2007' — a primary source that contradicts Portuguese Wikipedia's 2015 launch claim (2015 may reflect when regular use began, but no source supports it). The channel passed one million subscribers by his death.

events.title: The documentary O Jardim das Aflições premieres
events.text: Josias Teófilo's debut feature about Olavo's life and thought, named after the 1995 book, first screened at Virginia Commonwealth University with Olavo present. An October 2017 screening at UFPE was disrupted — an episode sympathetic outlets described as violent repression (attributed; that account's link is unverified). The film had a limited Brazilian theatrical release from 31 May–1 June 2017 (Brasília, Porto Alegre, Rio, São Paulo) per AdoroCinema's own dated news desk — which contradicts the '2015' label on AdoroCinema's film page.

events.title: Mídia Sem Máscara goes offline
events.text: Per Calil (2021), the site operated 2002–2017.

events.title: Near-fatal pneumonia; surgery removes the congenital tracheal tumor
events.text: In March 2018 a pneumonia he said 'nearly killed him' put him in hospital for about a month, and surgeons removed the congenital tracheal cyst the infection had inflamed (his own posts of 23–26 March, mirrored by the fan archive; reported by Boletim da Liberdade). His fullest account came in April 2021: born with a tracheal tumor that lay dormant until it broke the trachea at 71, an emergency operation at the VCU hospital with tumor removal and tracheal reconstruction, and recurring aftereffects that re-hospitalized him — two days in February 2020, again in early 2021. This is the 'old operation' of his c. 2020 lecture recollection, and the same congenital tumor he had described in a lecture of January 2010 — the point where his own telling, the lecture record and the press coverage all meet.

events.title: Bolsonaro's victory-night table displays O Mínimo
events.text: In his election-night livestream, Jair Bolsonaro kept on the table a Bible, the Constitution, a Churchill biography and O Mínimo que Você Precisa Saber para Não Ser um Idiota — widely read by the press as signaling Olavo's status as intellectual reference of the incoming government (that reading is the press's).

events.title: Ernesto Araújo named foreign minister; the press attributes the choice to Olavo
events.text: Fox News (14 November 2018) and other outlets reported Bolsonaro chose the little-known diplomat after Olavo recommended him. Attribution of ministerial picks to Olavo — Araújo at Itamaraty, Ricardo Vélez Rodríguez and later Abraham Weintraub at Education — is a press and academic characterization (Calil 2021; Gazeta do Povo calls him the ministers' 'guru'), which Olavo himself alternately embraced and dismissed.

events.title: The Bolsonaro government takes office with ministers labeled 'olavistas'
events.text: Academics and commentators (Calil 2021; Castro Rocha 2021) describe the Education and Foreign Affairs ministries as staffed on Olavo's recommendation; the press routinely labeled him the government's 'guru' or 'ideologue' — a title he publicly rejected, and which the scholar Mark Sedgwick also considers overstated. Sedgwick (2021), citing an Estado de S. Paulo interview of 24 November 2018, records the specifics: Carvalho was offered the education ministry and refused it, recommending instead his long-time friend Ricardo Vélez Rodríguez, and recommended the career diplomat Ernesto Araújo — who shared his interest in Traditionalism — for foreign minister.

events.title: Awarded the Grã-Cruz of the Ordem de Rio Branco
events.text: Decree published in an extra edition of the Diário Oficial da União on 30 April 2019, giving him the order's highest rank alongside state authorities; Flávio and Eduardo Bolsonaro received the lower Grande Oficial rank in the same decree. A bill in the Chamber of Deputies later sought to annul the concession as contrary to the order's rules — the award remained contested.

events.title: Launch of the online newspaper Brasil Sem Medo
events.text: Announced on 6 December 2019 and live from 19 December 2019, with Olavo as figurehead — reported independently by Metrópoles and Gazeta do Povo; the site is in the Wayback record by 26 December 2019.

events.title: Court upholds R$ 2.9 million owed to Caetano Veloso
events.text: Consultor Jurídico reported that his appeal failed against accumulated daily fines plus R$ 65,000 in moral damages, for refusing to delete 2017 social-media posts about the musician Caetano Veloso that the courts had found defamatory. In 2024 CartaCapital reported his heirs were notified of the debt.

events.title: Returns to Brazil for treatment: the InCor months
events.text: After the incomplete US bladder operation of May 2021 — two tumors removed, a second surgery needed, by his own account — he flew to Brazil in early July. His only stated reason: 'Brazilian medicine is better than American' (post of 9 July). Taken ill on the flight, he entered InCor (Hospital das Clínicas, USP) on 8 July with cardiac ischemia per the hospital bulletin, and on 13 July underwent a three-hour emergency surgery for urethral obstruction, revising the May operation (the bulletin gives 13 July; some later summaries say 15 July). Discharged on the 18th, he was readmitted on 9 August: the press reported urinary infection, sepsis, ICU and intermittent hemodialysis, while a family statement of 19 August denied infection and ICU — a documented contradiction between entourage messaging and the hospital record that prefigures the January cause-of-death dispute. He remained hospitalized in São Paulo into late October ('fearsome diseases subjected me to a complex succession of surgeries', post of 26 October).

events.title: Returns to the United States after treatment in Brazil
events.text: Returned to the US on 17 November 2021, after four months hospitalized in São Paulo (Folha PE; Poder360's obituary timeline).

events.title: The rift with the government, in his own dated words
events.text: It began, in his own telling, the day Sérgio Moro left the government: if he really were the government's guru, 'none of this would have happened' — Bolsonaro had never asked his advice (24 April 2020, reported the same day by Correio Braziliense). Through 2020–21 his target was the military wing: the public attack on Gen. Ramos in the Weintraub crisis (May–June 2020), and 'it is obvious the generals never supported the president' in defense of chancellor Ernesto Araújo four days before Araújo fell (March 2021) — every characterization his own. In December 2021, weeks before his death, he called Bolsonaro's re-election bid a lost fight in live remarks (20 December) and said he would vote for Bolsonaro only 'for lack of alternatives' (28 December). Metrópoles' posthumous report that he 'died resentful' of the Bolsonaro family caps the same arc.

events.title: COVID-19 diagnosis announced; course classes suspended
events.text: A message on his Telegram channel dated 15 January 2022 announced the diagnosis and the cancellation of his course classes. Some international outlets date the announcement to 16 January — a minor discrepancy the sources leave open.

events.title: Dies in hospital, aged 74
events.text: The family's statement, posted to his social accounts in the early hours of 25 January, said he died 'na noite de 24 de janeiro' and gave no cause; no official cause of death was ever released. The cause was publicly disputed: his daughter Heloísa — publicly estranged from her father for years — said he 'died of Covid'; his personal physician, Ahmed Youssif El Tassa, stated the death resulted from acute respiratory failure caused by pulmonary emphysema, a chronic condition, associated with congestive heart failure, bacterial pneumonia from methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and generalized infection, and was 'not related to COVID'; critical outlets noted the COVID diagnosis announced days earlier and his public minimization of the pandemic. His own lectures had recounted a lifelong pulmonary history — bedridden through his first seven years and, in a c. 2020 lecture, decades of asymptomatic emphysema after an old lung operation (per the community transcriptions). Each position is its author's; this site does not adjudicate between them.

events.title: Bolsonaro decrees one day of official national mourning
events.text: The decree of 25 January 2022 declared official mourning throughout Brazil 'as a sign of grief for the death of Professor Olavo Luiz Pimentel de Carvalho'; Bolsonaro called him 'one of the greatest thinkers in the history of our country'. It was only the second mourning decree of his term.

events.title: Burial at St. Joseph's Cemetery, Petersburg, Virginia
events.text: Buried on 26 January 2022 at St. Joseph's Cemetery, Petersburg, Virginia — the ceremony reported same-day by Metrópoles and by Correio Braziliense/Folhapress.

events.title: Posthumous honors: the Biblioteca Nacional medal, then Curitiba
events.text: In July 2022 the Biblioteca Nacional's Medalha — Ordem do Mérito do Livro honored him posthumously, his widow Roxane receiving it (the family-side archive shows her at the ceremony on 2 July). That year's honors list was itself contested: writers publicly refused their medals over other honorees in the same batch, and the critical coverage that confirms his homage folded his death back into the cause dispute in the same sentence. On 25 April 2023 the Curitiba city council held a posthumous tribute session and moved a grant of honorary citizenship.

events.title: Heirs notified over the Caetano Veloso judgment debt
events.text: In early September 2023 the courts notified his heirs of the R$ 2.9 million owed to Caetano Veloso — reported by NSC Total (5 September) and Bahia Notícias (6 September); the CartaCapital article is in the Wayback record on 5 September 2023. The dataset previously carried this as 2024, an error introduced by a later related report.

figures.name: Roxane Andrade de Souza
figures.role: Widow; received his posthumous Biblioteca Nacional medal (July 2022)

figures.name: Heloísa de Carvalho
figures.role: Eldest daughter, publicly estranged from her father for years and excluded from his will; stated after his death that he 'died of Covid', which his personal physician publicly denied. Found dead at her home in Atibaia, São Paulo, in January 2026; the cause was not disclosed

figures.name: Jair Bolsonaro
figures.role: President of Brazil 2019–2022; decreed national mourning at Olavo's death. The press called Olavo his 'guru' — a label Olavo rejected; Metrópoles reported (attributed) that he 'died resentful' of the Bolsonaro family after their public estrangement from 2020–2021

figures.name: Flávio and Eduardo Bolsonaro
figures.role: Presidential sons and public admirers; Calil dates the family's approach to Olavo to c. 2012–2013. Both received the Ordem de Rio Branco (Grande Oficial) in the same 2019 decree that gave Olavo the Grã-Cruz

figures.name: Ernesto Araújo
figures.role: Foreign minister 2019–2021; his appointment was widely attributed to Olavo's recommendation (Fox News, November 2018)

figures.name: Ricardo Vélez Rodríguez
figures.role: Education minister January–April 2019; appointment attributed by press and academics to Olavo's recommendation

figures.name: Abraham Weintraub
figures.role: Education minister 2019–2020; commonly described as an Olavo-endorsed pick (Gazeta do Povo calls Olavo the 'guru' of ministers Araújo and Weintraub)

figures.name: Aleksandr Dugin
figures.role: Russian ideologue; opponent in the 2011 written debate published as Os EUA e a Nova Ordem Mundial (2012)

figures.name: Frithjof Schuon
figures.role: Perennialist master; per Sedgwick, appointed Olavo his muqaddam for Brazil in Bloomington in 1986, before Olavo broke with him and became a fierce critic of perennialism

figures.name: Padre Paulo Ricardo de Azevedo Jr.
figures.role: Catholic priest (Cuiabá) and media figure; by Olavo's own dated account (lecture of 30 October 2010), his personal confessor — the best-documented figure of his return to full Catholic practice; the two later collaborated publicly

figures.name: Josias Teófilo
figures.role: Director of the documentary O Jardim das Aflições (2017), his debut feature

figures.name: Juan Alfredo César Muller
figures.role: Argentine psychiatrist and astrologer; Olavo's entry into astrology — asked him to edit a book in the late 1970s, and Olavo assisted his 1978 astrology course at PUC-SP (per Sedgwick 2021, corroborating the tertiary account)

figures.name: Stanislavs Ladusans
figures.role: Jesuit philosopher; Olavo studied three years at his Conjunto de Pesquisa Filosófica (Conpefil, PUC-Rio), leaving when Ladusans died in 1993 and the group closed

figures.name: Ahmed Youssif El Tassa
figures.role: Personal physician; publicly stated the death was from respiratory failure due to emphysema and associated conditions, 'not related to COVID'

figures.name: Felipe Moura Brasil
figures.role: Journalist; selected and organized the 193 articles of O Mínimo (2013)

figures.name: Caetano Veloso
figures.role: Musician; won cumulative fines and damages (R$ 2.9 million upheld in 2020) over 2017 posts the courts found defamatory

figures.name: Mark Sedgwick
figures.role: Historian of Traditionalism (Aarhus University); his 2021 Aries article is the fullest academic account of Olavo's Traditionalist and Maryamiyya years, and he coined the 'post-Traditionalist' characterization

figures.name: Gilberto Calil

disambiguation.note: Almost everything about this subject is contested terrain — his title, his influence, his death, and his own retellings of his trajectory. This section records the distinctions the sources themselves make.

items.title: olavodecarvalho.org is no longer his site
items.text: As of August 2026 the live domain returns a page of unrelated e-commerce spam (apparently lapsed and squatted). His actual site must be cited via Internet Archive snapshots (e.g. the 15 December 2021 capture). Do not link the live domain as an official site.

items.title: 'Philosopher' is a claimed and contested title
items.text: He styled himself a philosopher and taught philosophy for decades, but held no degree in the field (he left PUC-Rio's Conpefil without completing studies); mainstream obituaries write 'self-described philosopher', his students insist on the title without qualification. This site records who calls him what.

items.title: Two works named O Jardim das Aflições
items.text: The 1995 book (Diadorim) and the 2017 documentary about him (dir. Josias Teófilo) share the name; AdoroCinema additionally mislabels the film as 2015.

items.title: Not the other Carvalhos
items.text: Not the historian José Murilo de Carvalho (d. 2023), the poet Ronald de Carvalho, or the politician Salatiel Carvalho — search results routinely conflate them.

items.title: 'Guru of Bolsonaro' is an attributed label
items.text: The international press (NYT: 'Bolsonaro's Far-Right Guru') and much of the Brazilian press used the label; Olavo publicly rejected it, and the scholar Mark Sedgwick considers it overstated. It appears on this site only as someone's characterization, never in the site's own voice.

items.title: The COF corpus is cited, not reproduced
items.text: The Curso Online de Filosofia's community transcriptions (585 lectures) are public and of varying review quality, and the lecture header dates carry known defects. This project cites lectures by aula number and date only; the reception index in data/cof-reception.json records which lectures engage which philosopher.

philosophers.intro: The twenty philosophers most engaged by the Curso Online de Filosofia, by measured presence in the 585-lecture corpus. Each page carries the thinker's own life and works, and the record of which lectures engage him.

philosophers.name: Aristóteles
philosophers.summary: Greek philosopher, disciple of Plato and tutor of Alexander of Macedon, founder of the Lyceum in Athens. His surviving treatises cover logic, physics, biology, metaphysics, ethics, politics, rhetoric and poetics, and shaped much of ancient, medieval and modern philosophy.

timeline.label: Born in Stagira, a small city of Chalcidice in northern Greece.
Moves to Athens and enters Plato's Academy, where he remains for about twenty years as disciple and colleague.
On Plato's death, leaves Athens and settles in Assos, in Asia Minor, with the ruler Hermias.
In Assos and then on the island of Lesbos, pursues research in marine biology; marries Pythias, Hermias's niece.
Summoned by Philip II to the Macedonian court at Pella, becomes tutor of the king's son, the future Alexander the Great (Britannica records 343 or 342 BC).
Returns to Athens and founds his own school, the Lyceum, by the gymnasium dedicated to Apollo Lyceus.

The Lyceum period: composition and organization of most of the surviving corpus — among others the Organon (logic), the Physics, the Metaphysics, the Nicomachean Ethics, the Politics and the Poetics; the internal dating of the treatises is uncertain and debated by specialists.
On Alexander's death and the anti-Macedonian reaction in Athens, withdraws from the city to Chalcis, on the island of Euboea.
Dies in Chalcis, Euboea.

philosophers.name: Descartes
philosophers.summary: French philosopher, mathematician and scientist, often described as the founder of modern philosophy. He created analytic geometry, formulated the first modern version of mind–body dualism, and proposed a method of systematic doubt as the foundation of knowledge.

timeline.label: Born in La Haye, in the Touraine region of France.
Studies at the Jesuit college of La Flèche, following the curriculum of grammar, humanities and scholastic philosophy.
Takes a degree in law at the University of Poitiers, which he will never practice.
Becomes a volunteer soldier at Breda, in the service of Prince Maurice of Nassau; decisive encounter with the scientist Isaac Beeckman.
In the region of Ulm, has the three dreams he interprets as a life mission devoted to the reform of knowledge.
Abandons the Rules for the Direction of the Mind (unfinished) and settles in the Netherlands, where he lives most of his adult life.
Publishes the Discourse on Method, together with the essays Dioptrics, Meteors and Geometry.
Publishes the Meditations on First Philosophy, with the Objections and Replies (2nd edition 1642).
Publishes the Principles of Philosophy, the synthesis of his metaphysics and natural philosophy.
Publishes The Passions of the Soul; accepts Queen Christina of Sweden's invitation and moves to Stockholm.
Dies in Stockholm, after falling ill in the Swedish winter.

philosophers.name: Platão
philosophers.summary: Athenian philosopher, disciple of Socrates and teacher of Aristotle, founder of the Academy. His dialogues, which put into circulation themes such as the theory of Forms, the immortality of the soul and the just city, are among the founding texts of Western philosophy.

timeline.label: Born in Athens to an aristocratic family (the SEP gives '429?'; recent scholarship cited in the SEP's Socrates chronology proposes 424/423 BC).
Death of Socrates, to whose circle Plato belonged; after the execution he leaves Athens and spends a period in Megara, followed by travels the tradition attributes to him (Cyrene, Italy, Egypt).
First journey to Italy and Sicily; in Syracuse he attaches himself to Dion, brother-in-law of the tyrant Dionysius I.
Back in Athens, founds the Academy, the school Britannica places in the 380s BC and describes as a remote ancestor of the modern university.
Dialogues of the so-called early (Socratic) period, on the usual stylometric chronology: Apology, Crito, Euthyphro, Laches, Charmides, Gorgias, Protagoras, among others.
Dialogues of the middle period, including the Phaedo, the Symposium and the Republic (books II–X), in which the theory of Forms is articulated.
Second and third journeys to Syracuse, involving him with Dion in the attempt to influence the young tyrant Dionysius II — episodes narrated in the Seventh Letter, whose authenticity is disputed.
Late dialogues, among them the Theaetetus, Sophist, Statesman, Timaeus, Philebus and the Laws; the corpus transmitted under his name also includes letters and works of disputed authenticity.
Dies in Athens at about eighty; according to Diogenes Laertius he was buried at the Academy.

philosophers.name: Marx
philosophers.summary: German philosopher, economist and revolutionary, author (with Friedrich Engels) of the Communist Manifesto and of Capital. His theory of history, his critique of political economy and the political movement he inspired profoundly marked the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

timeline.label: Born in Trier, in the Rhine province of Prussia.
Enters the University of Bonn (October 1835) and transfers the following year to Berlin, where he studies law and philosophy.
Takes his doctorate in philosophy from the University of Jena.
Becomes editor of the Rheinische Zeitung in Cologne.
Marries Jenny von Westphalen (June) and moves to Paris months later.
Expelled from France, settles in Brussels, followed by Engels; from this period date the manuscripts of The German Ideology (1845–46), published posthumously.
Publishes the Communist Manifesto with Engels, in the year of the European revolutions.
Expelled from Paris once more, settles in London, his home for the rest of his life.
Publishes A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy, whose Preface carries the classic formulation of his materialist conception of history.

Foundation of the International Working Men's Association (First International); neither its founder nor its head, Marx becomes its leading intellectual figure, drafting the inaugural address and the provisional statutes.
Publishes volume I of Capital (volumes II and III would appear posthumously, in 1885 and 1894, edited by Engels).
Dies in London.

philosophers.name: Tomás de Aquino
philosophers.place: Roccasecca, near Aquino (Kingdom of Sicily, present-day Italy)
philosophers.summary: Dominican friar, theologian and philosopher, the leading figure of thirteenth-century scholasticism. His synthesis of Aristotelian philosophy and Christian doctrine, set out above all in the Summa theologiae and the Summa contra gentiles, became a central reference of the Catholic tradition.

timeline.label: Born at Roccasecca, a castle of a noble family near Aquino, between Rome and Naples (the SEP gives 'around 1225'; Britannica, '1224/25').
Studies as a child at the Benedictine abbey of Monte Cassino, where his family expected him to make his career.

As an adolescent student at the University of Naples, decides to join the newly founded Order of Preachers (Dominicans) at about twenty; his family, opposed, keeps him detained at Roccasecca for about a year before relenting.
Studies philosophy in Paris as a Dominican friar; in 1248 he is sent to Cologne, under the direction of Albert the Great.
Nominated by Albert, returns to Paris for the advanced degree in theology; composes the commentary on Peter Lombard's Sentences (Scriptum, 1252–56).
Master of theology, holds the Dominican chair at the University of Paris.
Back in Italy, teaches in Dominican houses; composes the Summa contra gentiles (c. 1258–64, per Britannica).
Begins the Summa theologiae, his greatest work, left unfinished at his death (1265/66–73, per Britannica).
Second Paris regency, marked by the controversies over radical Aristotelianism ('Averroism'); writes commentaries on Aristotle's principal works.
Returns to Italy, to Naples, where he spends his last teaching years.
Dies at the Cistercian abbey of Fossanova, in Lazio.

philosophers.name: Kant
philosophers.summary: German philosopher, a central figure of modern philosophy, who spent his whole life in Königsberg. His 'critical philosophy', set out in the three Critiques, proposed that human reason legislates both for the knowledge of nature and for morality.

timeline.label: Born in Königsberg, capital of East Prussia.
Studies at the University of Königsberg (the Albertina); after university, works for some years as a private tutor in the region.
Takes the degree of Magister and becomes Privatdozent (private lecturer) at Königsberg, a position he holds for fifteen years under a heavy teaching load.
Appointed full professor of logic and metaphysics at Königsberg; presents the Inaugural Dissertation, the landmark of his critical turn.
Publishes the Critique of Pure Reason (revised 2nd edition 1787).
Publishes the Prolegomena to Any Future Metaphysics.
Publishes the Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, his principal work on the fundamental principle of morality.
Publishes the Critique of Practical Reason.
Publishes the Critique of the Power of Judgment.
Publishes The Metaphysics of Morals (Doctrine of Right and Doctrine of Virtue), after Toward Perpetual Peace (1795).
Dies in Königsberg, the city he never left for long.

philosophers.name: Sócrates
philosophers.summary: Athenian philosopher who wrote nothing, known through the testimonies of Plato, Xenophon and Aristophanes. His practice of interrogating fellow citizens about the virtues, and his condemnation to death for impiety, made him a founding figure of Western philosophical ethics.

timeline.label: Born in Athens, in the deme of Alopece (the SEP, following Nails, gives 469 BC; Britannica records c. 470 BC).
Serves as an infantry soldier (hoplite) in the Potidaea campaign, alongside Alcibiades.
Outbreak of the Peloponnesian War between Athens and Sparta, the backdrop of his adult life.
Fights at the battle of Delium, an Athenian defeat, under the command of Laches.
Caricatured in Aristophanes' comedy The Clouds, staged at the festival of Dionysus.
Fights at the battle of Amphipolis, another Athenian disaster — his last known campaign.
A member of the presiding committee (prytaneis) by lot, opposes the collective, summary trial of the generals of the battle of Arginusae before the Assembly.
Under the regime of the Thirty, refuses the order to go to Salamis and arrest the democratic general Leon — an episode later recalled in his defense.

Works: he wrote nothing; his thought is known above all through Plato's dialogues, Xenophon's Socratic writings and Aristophanes' satire — the disparity between the portraits constitutes the 'Socratic problem'.
Tried for impiety and for corrupting the young, he is condemned and executed by poison (hemlock) at seventy, in Athens.

philosophers.name: René Guénon
philosophers.summary: French metaphysician and writer, the principal formulator of the twentieth-century 'Traditionalist' or 'Perennialist' current. He wrote on Eastern metaphysics, symbolism, initiation and the critique of the modern world; he embraced Islam and lived his last twenty years in Cairo.

timeline.label: Born in Blois, France; raised in a strict Catholic milieu and educated by Jesuits.
After mathematics studies in Paris (Collège Rollin), abandons preparation for the academic examinations.
Frequents the Parisian occultist and neo-spiritualist milieux — the most obscure period of his biography.
Founds the occultist review La Gnose, which publishes his first writings, already conversant with Vedanta.
Marries a devout Catholic; a new phase of withdrawal from the occultist circles and association with Catholic intellectuals (among them Jacques Maritain).
Publishes his first book, Introduction générale à l'étude des doctrines hindoues, and the critique Le Théosophisme: histoire d'une pseudo-religion; L'Erreur spirite follows in 1923.
Publishes Orient et Occident.
Publishes L'Homme et son devenir selon le Vêdânta, his axial work on Vedanta; L'Ésotérisme de Dante is from the same year.
Publishes La Crise du monde moderne and Le Roi du monde; Catholic criticism of the latter deepens his estrangement from the Church.
Sudden death of his wife.
Travels to Cairo for a three-month stay and remains until his death; openly embraces Islam, is initiated into the Shadhiliyya Sufi order under the name Abdel Wahed Yahya, and remarries.
Publishes Le Règne de la Quantité et les Signes des Temps, considered his masterpiece of the critique of modernity.
Dies in Cairo, Egypt.

philosophers.name: Hegel
philosophers.summary: German philosopher, the leading exponent of post-Kantian German idealism. He elaborated a system spanning logic, philosophy of nature and philosophy of spirit, with lasting influence on philosophy, political theory and the historiography of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

timeline.label: Born in Stuttgart, in the duchy of Württemberg.
Studies at the Protestant seminary of Tübingen (the Stift), where he forms friendships with the poet Hölderlin and the philosopher Schelling.
Moves to Jena, joining Schelling, and publishes his first philosophical work (on the difference between Fichte's and Schelling's systems), along with the dissertation on the orbits of the planets.
Publishes the Phenomenology of Spirit, completed at Jena.
Publishes the Science of Logic, in parts (1812, 1813 and 1816).
Returns to university life as professor at Heidelberg.
Publishes the Encyclopedia of the Philosophical Sciences, the systematic exposition of his thought, later revised in new editions.
Takes the chair of philosophy at the University of Berlin, the most prestigious in the German philosophical world.
Publishes in Berlin the Elements of the Philosophy of Right, his major work of political philosophy.
Dies in Berlin, at the height of his fame.

philosophers.name: Louis Lavelle
philosophers.summary: French philosopher, one of the principal French metaphysicians of the twentieth century and a representative of the 'philosophie de l'esprit' current. Professor at the Sorbonne and the Collège de France, he developed an ontology of participation in being, articulated in the tetralogy La dialectique de l'éternel présent.

timeline.label: Born in Saint-Martin-de-Villeréal, in the Lot-et-Garonne, France.
Teaching career that passes through the University of Strasbourg, before the Sorbonne and the Collège de France.
Publishes La Dialectique du monde sensible.
Professor of philosophy at the Sorbonne.
Publishes La Conscience de soi.
Publishes La Présence totale.
Publishes Le Mal et la souffrance.
Appointed inspector-general of national education and elected to the Collège de France, where he teaches from 1941 to 1951 (a chair opened with the inaugural lecture L'existence et la valeur).
Publishes Du temps et de l'éternité, volume III of the tetralogy La dialectique de l'éternel présent (whose central volume, De l'Acte, is considered his principal work).
Publishes Introduction à l'ontologie; elected to the Académie des sciences morales et politiques.
Dies in the Lot-et-Garonne (Britannica records Saint-Martin-de-Villeréal as the place of death; French sources give neighboring Parranquet).

philosophers.name: Nietzsche
philosophers.summary: German philosopher and cultural critic, trained as a classical philologist, who published intensely through the 1870s and 1880s. He is known for his radical critiques of traditional European morality, religion and philosophy, and for concepts such as the will to power, the eternal recurrence and the Übermensch. His productive career ended abruptly with the mental collapse of 1889.

timeline.label: Born in Röcken, near Leipzig, son of a Lutheran pastor.
At 24, called to the chair of classical philology at the University of Basel — the youngest ever appointed to such a post; in his student years at Leipzig he had met Richard Wagner.
Publishes his first book, The Birth of Tragedy, a polemic that breaks with conventional philological scholarship.
Publishes Human, All Too Human, the landmark of his 'positivist' phase and of the break with Wagner.
Resigns the Basel chair for health reasons; begins the decade of itinerant life between Switzerland, Italy and France, devoted to writing.
Publishes The Gay Science (expanded second edition 1887), where the announcement of the 'death of God' first appears.
Publishes Thus Spoke Zarathustra, in four parts.
Publishes Beyond Good and Evil (1886) and On the Genealogy of Morality (1887), central works of his maturity.
Last productive year: writes Twilight of the Idols, The Case of Wagner and other final texts.
Suffers a mental collapse in Turin; spends his final years in the care of his mother and then his sister, in deepening silence.
Dies in Weimar, of a stroke complicated by pneumonia; his sister Elisabeth takes control of his literary estate.

philosophers.name: Leibniz
philosophers.summary: German polymath — philosopher, mathematician, jurist and diplomat — counted among the great rationalists of the seventeenth century. He developed the differential and integral calculus independently of Newton and formulated a metaphysical system centered on the monads and pre-established harmony. He spent most of his career in the service of the House of Hanover.

timeline.label: Born in Leipzig (21 June by the Julian calendar then in use; 1 July by the Gregorian, as Britannica records).
Enters the University of Leipzig, beginning his formation in philosophy and law.
Completes his doctorate in law; the same year he meets Baron von Boineburg, who secures him a position at the court of the Elector of Mainz.
Diplomatic mission in Paris, then the center of European science, with a brief journey to London (1673); he frequents the leading savants of the age.
Lays the foundations of the differential and integral calculus, per Britannica.
Enters the service of the House of Hanover as librarian to Duke Johann Friedrich; on the way, meets Spinoza in Amsterdam (18–21 November).
Writes the Discourse on Metaphysics and begins the correspondence with Arnauld, central expositions of his mature metaphysics.
Publishes the Essays of Theodicy, the only philosophical book he published in his lifetime.
Writes the Monadology and the Principles of Nature and Grace, final syntheses of his system; that year his patron Georg Ludwig becomes George I of England, but Leibniz remains in Hanover.
Dies in Hanover.

philosophers.name: Mário Ferreira dos Santos
philosophers.summary: Brazilian philosopher, translator and writer, creator of the system he named 'concrete philosophy'. In little more than fifteen years he published the monumental Enciclopédia de Ciências Filosóficas e Sociais, in dozens of volumes, working outside the university establishment. He fell into relative obscurity after his death and has been republished since the 2000s, with the rights to his work acquired by the publisher É Realizações.

timeline.label: Born in Tietê (SP), son of the Portuguese Francisco Dias Ferreira dos Santos, a theatrical entrepreneur and cinema pioneer established in Pelotas (RS).
Appears, still a child, in his father's silent film 'Os óculos do vovô', one of the oldest Brazilian films known.
Early schooling at the Ginásio Gonzaga, the Jesuit college of Pelotas; at 14 he wishes to enter the Society of Jesus but is counseled against it.
Studies at the Law Faculty of Porto Alegre, graduating in 1930; begins writing for newspapers of Pelotas and Porto Alegre (Diário de Notícias, Correio do Povo).
Works as a journalist; after the Revolution of 1930, is jailed for criticism of the new regime.
Hired by Livraria do Globo as a translator from Latin, Greek, German and French; translates Aristotle, Nietzsche, Kant, Pascal and Thomas Aquinas, among others.
Moves to São Paulo, continuing his work as a translator at Editora Flama.

Begins, with Filosofia e Cosmovisão, the publication of the Enciclopédia de Ciências Filosóficas e Sociais, the systematic project that would occupy the rest of his life (counts of the total vary: 45 and more than 50 volumes are both cited).

Publishes the encyclopedia's introductory volumes at speed: Lógica e Dialética (1953), Psicologia (1953), Teoria do Conhecimento (1954), Ontologia e Cosmologia (1954), Tratado de Simbólica (1956), Filosofia da Crise (1956), O Homem Perante o Infinito (1956) and Noologia Geral (1956).
Publishes Filosofia Concreta, the tenth work of the series, in which he establishes his own way of philosophizing and the core of his system.
Dies, leaving the encyclopedia almost entirely published and a vast body of work partly unpublished.
His work returns to circulation: the publisher É Realizações acquires the rights and republishes his books, among them A Invasão Vertical dos Bárbaros (repub. 2012).

philosophers.name: Santo Agostinho
philosophers.summary: Bishop of Hippo and one of the most influential Christian thinkers of all time, the bridge between ancient philosophy and medieval thought. A professor of rhetoric converted to ascetic Christianity in 386, he left more than five million words of surviving writings, among them the Confessions and The City of God.

timeline.label: Born in Thagaste, in Roman Africa (present-day Souk Ahras, Algeria), son of Monica, a devout Christian, and Patricius, baptized only on his deathbed.
Becomes a 'hearer' (auditor) of Manichaeism, the dualist religion of Persian origin, to which he remains attached for about a decade.
Moves to Italy and takes up in Milan, then capital of the Western Empire, the public post of professor of rhetoric and panegyrist of the imperial court (the SEP dates the move to Milan to 383).
Converts to ascetic Christianity and renounces the chair of rhetoric and his career prospects.
At the rural retreat of Cassiciacum, near Milan, writes his first philosophical dialogues (Contra Academicos, De beata vita, De ordine).
Baptized by Ambrose in Milan; on the return to Africa, his mother dies at Ostia (388).
Ordained a priest at Hippo Regius (present-day Annaba, Algeria), apparently against his own wishes.
Becomes bishop of Hippo — Britannica gives 395 or 396; the SEP, about 396.
Writes the Confessions, 'philosophy in autobiography' — the SEP dates the work to c. 396–400; Britannica, to c. 400.
Writes The City of God, his great work of the theology of history, begun after the sack of Rome.
Dies at Hippo Regius, aged 75.

philosophers.name: Eric Voegelin
philosophers.summary: German-American political philosopher, formed in Vienna, who fled Nazism in 1938 and made his career in the United States and Munich. He sought a comprehensive philosophy of man, society and history, and became known for his analysis of modern political movements as 'gnosticism'. His principal works include The New Science of Politics and the Order and History series.

timeline.label: Born in Cologne, Germany; the family later moves to Vienna, where he receives his entire formation.
Obtains the habilitation and begins teaching at the University of Vienna (Britannica records his teaching at the Law Faculty from 1929 to 1938).
Publishes two books critically analyzing racism and race ideas, which set him against Nazism.
Publishes Der autoritäre Staat (The Authoritarian State).
After the Anschluss, flees Austria with his wife, passing through Switzerland before emigrating to the United States.
Professor at Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge; becomes a US citizen in 1944.
Publishes The New Science of Politics, the work that projects him into the American intellectual debate.
Publishes the first three volumes of Order and History; volume 4 appears in 1974 and the posthumous volume 5 in 1987.
Takes up in Munich the former chair of Max Weber in political science at the Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität.
Publishes Anamnesis: Zur Theorie der Geschichte und Politik, central to his philosophy of consciousness.
Returns to the United States as senior research fellow at the Hoover Institution, Stanford University.
Dies at Stanford, California.

philosophers.name: Husserl
philosophers.summary: A mathematician by training and the founder of phenomenology, the movement that marked all of twentieth-century continental philosophy. He made his career at Halle, Göttingen and Freiburg, where Heidegger succeeded him. Of Jewish origin, he spent his last years excluded from German university life under the Nazi regime.

timeline.label: Born in Proßnitz, Moravia, then in the Austrian Empire (present-day Prostějov, Czechia).
Takes his doctorate in mathematics in Vienna with a thesis on the calculus of variations; works briefly as Weierstrass's assistant in Berlin.
Privatdozent at the University of Halle for fourteen years; in 1891 publishes his first book, Philosophy of Arithmetic.
Publishes the Logical Investigations, the founding work of phenomenology.
Professor at Göttingen (extraordinarius from 1901, ordinarius from 1906), a position secured by the success of the Investigations.
Publishes Ideas for a Pure Phenomenology (Ideas I), the transcendental turn of his thought.
Takes the chair of philosophy at Freiburg, succeeding the neo-Kantian Heinrich Rickert; Edith Stein becomes his assistant.
Retires at Freiburg, succeeded by Heidegger; shortly afterwards delivers in Paris the lectures that would become the Cartesian Meditations.

With the arrival of Nazism, suffers the exclusion imposed on Jews in Germany — in a letter of 4 May 1933 he speaks of the erection of a 'spiritual ghetto' in which he and his children were being enclosed.
Publishes (in part) The Crisis of European Sciences and Transcendental Phenomenology, developed from lectures in Vienna and Prague.
Dies in Freiburg im Breisgau.

philosophers.name: Heidegger
philosophers.summary: A central figure of twentieth-century European philosophy, author of Being and Time (1927) and renewer of the question of the meaning of being. Husserl's disciple and successor at Freiburg, he influenced existentialism, hermeneutics and deconstruction. His involvement with Nazism — the 1933–34 rectorate and party membership until 1945 — remains an object of controversy.

timeline.label: Born in Messkirch, in the Black Forest region of Germany.
Becomes associate professor at the University of Marburg, where he teaches ontology, logic and the history of philosophy until 1928.
Publishes Being and Time, his greatest work, and is promoted to full professor at Marburg.
Appointed to the Freiburg chair previously held by Rickert and by Husserl, whose successor he becomes.
Elected rector of the University of Freiburg after Hitler's seizure of power; joins the Nazi Party on 1 May and conducts the 'alignment' (Gleichschaltung) of the university.
Resigns the rectorate, but remains a party member until the end of the regime.
Delivers the great lecture courses on Nietzsche, later collected in book form; in the 1930s–40s he also lectures on Hölderlin, Schelling, Hegel and the pre-Socratics.
After Germany's surrender and the denazification hearings, the French military government bans him from all teaching and university activity.
The teaching ban is lifted, allowing him to assume emeritus status at Freiburg.
Publishes Holzwege (Off the Beaten Track), collecting essays from 1935–1946.
Dies in Freiburg im Breisgau.

philosophers.name: Frithjof Schuon
philosophers.summary: Swiss-German writer and metaphysician, the leading exponent of the perennialist (Traditionalist) school in the twentieth century alongside René Guénon and Ananda Coomaraswamy. Initiated into Sufism in Algeria in 1933, he directed from Europe — and, after 1980, from Bloomington, Indiana — the order that became known as the Maryamiyya, and wrote dozens of books on metaphysics, comparative religion and sacred art. The accounts of his life here follow chiefly his estate's site and the historian of Traditionalism Mark Sedgwick.

timeline.label: Born in Basel, Switzerland, son of a German violinist.
After his father's death, moves with his mother to Mulhouse, in French Alsace.
Settles in Paris, where he works and deepens his study of Arabic and of Eastern doctrines.

Travels to Mostaganem, Algeria, enters Islam and spends about four months at the zawiya of the Sufi shaykh Ahmad al-Alawi, from whom he receives initiation (the date per the estate's site; other reconstructions place the departure from Europe in late 1932).
Publishes his first book, in German: Leitgedanken zur Urbesinnung (Primordial Meditation).
Settles in Lausanne, Switzerland, his base for nearly four decades.
Publishes De l'Unité transcendante des religions, his first and best-known book in French, the classic formulation of the perennialist thesis.
Marries Catherine Feer; obtains Swiss citizenship shortly afterwards.
Travels to the American West at the invitation of Indigenous friends; on the 1959 visit he is adopted by the Sioux (and, in 1984, by the Crow).
Publishes mature works such as Logic and Transcendence, Form and Substance in the Religions and Esoterism as Principle and as Way.

Emigrates with his wife to the United States, settling in Bloomington, Indiana, near a community of disciples; in the first years there publishes From the Divine to the Human, To Have a Center and Roots of the Human Condition.

Becomes the target, in Bloomington, of accusations taken to a grand jury on the complaints of a former disciple; the prosecution dropped the charges shortly afterwards — an episode documented by the historian Mark Sedgwick in Against the Modern World (2004) and discussed on his academic blog.
Dies in Bloomington, Indiana.

philosophers.name: Ortega y Gasset
philosophers.summary: Spanish philosopher, essayist and intellectual leader, formed in German neo-Kantianism and creator of 'vital reason' ('I am I and my circumstance'). Professor of metaphysics in Madrid and founder of the Revista de Occidente, he became world-famous with The Revolt of the Masses. He left Spain with the Civil War and returned after the Second World War.

timeline.label: Born in Madrid, into a family tied to liberal journalism.
Studies in Germany — Leipzig, Berlin and, decisively, Marburg, under neo-Kantianism — before returning to Madrid.
Wins the competition (8 October) for the chair of metaphysics at the Central University of Madrid, vacant since the death of Nicolás Salmerón.
Publishes Meditaciones del Quijote, where the formula 'I am I and my circumstance' appears.
Publishes España invertebrada — the SEP dates the book to 1921; Britannica, to 1922.
Founds the Revista de Occidente, the leading organ of intellectual renewal in the Spain of the period.
Publishes La rebelión de las masas, his most famous work — Britannica dates it to 1929 (as a series of articles); the SEP records the book in 1930.
Becomes one of the first members of the Constituent Cortes of the Second Spanish Republic.
With the outbreak of the Civil War, leaves Spain; lives in Europe and Argentina, returning at the end of the Second World War (Britannica describes the period as voluntary exile).

Founds in Madrid, with his disciple Julián Marías, the Instituto de Humanidades — he never resumed his university chair, and the government restricts the institute's activities until its closure in 1950.
Dies in Madrid.

philosophers.name: Dante Alighieri
philosophers.fullName: Dante Alighieri (Durante di Alighiero degli Alighieri)
philosophers.summary: Poet, political thinker and 'father of the Italian language', author of the Divine Comedy, the poetic synthesis of medieval culture. He took an active part in the civic life of Florence until his condemnation to exile in 1302, and wrote in banishment his great prose works and the poem that immortalized him. He died in Ravenna in 1321.

timeline.label: Born in Florence — if he was indeed born under Gemini, as the Paradiso suggests, the birthday would fall between mid-May and mid-June (Britannica records c. 21 May–20 June).
By the testimony of his own writings, meets at age nine Beatrice Portinari, whom after her death (1290) he will invoke as the inspiration of his poetic vision.
Marries and starts a family; from then on takes part in Florence's cultural and civic life, serves as a soldier and holds various political offices.
Composes the Vita nuova, the prosimetrum in praise of Beatrice.
Condemned and exiled from Florence in the struggle between Guelph factions; he will never return to the city.
Writes the Convivio, abandoned with only four of the projected treatises, and De vulgari eloquentia, on the illustrious vernacular.
Composes the Divine Comedy (Inferno, Purgatorio, Paradiso), per Britannica's dating.
In the years of the expedition of Henry VII of Luxembourg, crowned emperor in 1312, becomes an impassioned propagandist of universal empire.
Writes the Monarchia, the Latin treatise on the necessity of an imperial power independent of the Church — its dating is disputed; the SEP considers composition after 1314 probable.
Moves from Verona (the court of Cangrande della Scala) to Ravenna, where he completes the Paradiso.
Dies in Ravenna — Britannica records the date as 13/14 September.

doctrines.note: Concepts Olavo de Carvalho named and taught as his own. This section is EXPOSITION, not endorsement: each entry says what he claimed, where he expounded it and when, and whom he credited. The project takes no view on whether any of it is true, exactly as the philosopher pages record his readings without adjudicating them. Summaries are the project's own words; his formulations are paraphrased rather than reproduced, and the few terms of art quoted are his coinages. Where a lecture date is unverified the entry says so, and where he revised a doctrine the revision is shown rather than smoothed into a single version.
doctrines.sourceNote: Drawn from the community transcription corpus of the course (585 lectures) and the video collection. A third of the fullest expositions sit in files the transcription project has not reviewed and that carry no date at all, so some entries below cite an undated lecture — that is a property of the corpus, not an omission here.

items.name: As doze camadas da personalidade
items.claim: A scheme of twelve demands that structure a human life, from taking possession of one's own body to standing before eternity. Each layer is a distinct kind of interest that can organise a person's whole existence, and he holds that most adults halt at the eighth, the crisis of maturity.
structure: As relações sociais e a linguagem
items.origin: Built in his Astrocaracterologia course (1990–92) from the twelve houses of the zodiac, taken as an ideal developmental circuit and grafted onto Szondi's drive psychology — which he said lacked any biographical dimension. He states three times that the scheme does not depend on astrology: he devised it to isolate precisely what a horoscope cannot describe.
items.revision: Presented as an evolutionary sequence in 2010 and 2014, then corrected in a later lecture: it is not an ideal development but the real structure of human existence, with all twelve demands pressing at once. He then distinguished the camada a person occupies from the etapa weighing on them. The diagram below shows twelve simultaneous demands for that reason.

expositions.where: a 133-minute class devoted to the scheme

items.name: Os eus — e a imortalidade da alma
items.claim: A distinction between the self that senses and acts now, the self others know, the self assembled from remembered life, and a permanent substantial self underneath — which he identifies flatly with the immortal soul, calling the other three merely its functions. The argument for immortality runs through that fourth term.
items.countNote: Often circulated as 'os cinco eus'. He says FOUR: searches for 'cinco eus', '5 eus' and 'quinto eu' return nothing across the whole corpus, while 'eu substancial' returns over a hundred occurrences, so the absence is real rather than a search artefact. A fifth term appears only if one counts the eternal 'Eu Sou', which he introduces as the ground constituting the fourth by concession — not as another item in the series.

items.name: Conhecimento por presença
items.claim: Beneath perception, memory and theory there is a prior, non-representational cognition that consists in reality simply being present to the knower. He calls it the most exact form of knowledge precisely because it cannot be turned into a thought one possesses. Its work is to explain how anyone ever corrects a framework from inside it: without it, he argues, a powerful philosophy would hypnotise its adherents completely and no school could revise itself.
items.lineageNote: He names Suhrawardī and the Persian's Philosophy of Illumination — but says he had grasped the thing before reading him, that Suhrawardī used the phrase not quite in his sense, and the attribution appears only seven months after he begins using the term. He states the channel himself: not Suhrawardī directly but Henry Corbin's chapters in En Islam Iranien. Guénon never co-occurs with the doctrine and Mullā Ṣadrā appears nowhere in the corpus, so the scholastic identification with ʿilm ḥuḍūrī is this project's gloss, not his. He also misdates Suhrawardī to the ninth century in a later lecture after dating him correctly to the twelfth in an earlier one.

items.name: Paralaxe cognitiva
items.claim: A displacement between the axis of a thinker's lived experience and the axis of his theoretical construction — seeing one thing while theorising another. He claims the phenomenon as his own discovery and insists it is a cognitive defect rather than hypocrisy or lying.
items.revision: He narrowed it by 2013 to strict performative self-refutation — where the act of saying something contradicts what is said — explicitly excluding mere self-contradiction, lying and propaganda, and presenting the narrowing as a correction of how his coinage was being used.

expositions.where: course lecture 40, on Marx as the worked example
a course announced under this name, Virginia

items.name: A teoria dos quatro discursos
items.claim: His most widely deployed framework: four kinds of discourse — poetic, rhetorical, dialectical and analytical — graded by the certainty they can carry, which he treats as one scale rather than four separate disciplines. He read the Aristotelian corpus in that order and held that Aristotle's logic becomes unintelligible once it is amputated from his rhetoric.

items.name: O círculo de latência
items.claim: The band of possibilities available to a person or a society at a given moment — what is not actual but could become so without a break in continuity. He uses it to argue that judging either a life or a historical situation requires knowing what was really open to it.

expositions.where: a course lecture titled after the concept

items.name: O método da confissão
items.claim: The procedure he called the core of his philosophy: philosophical work begins from an honest account of one's own actual state of knowledge and motive, rather than from a position adopted for argument. He grounds it in the Socratic examination and the Augustinian confession.

items.name: O horizonte de consciência
items.claim: The boundary of what a given consciousness can take in at all — which he calls a fundamental concept of his philosophy, and uses to explain why two people can face the same evidence and register different worlds.
items.caveat: Close to Lucien Goldmann's use of the term, a proximity he does not acknowledge.
